design_detail: Consensus evidence review by a 16-member expert committee of the US National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (published 12 January 2017), covering 11 health-endpoint areas. This card covers Chapter 7 (Respiratory Disease: pulmonary function, COPD, respiratory symptoms including chronic bronchitis, asthma), the lung cancer and head and neck cancer sections of Chapter 5 (Cancer) and Appendix B (Study Approach). Appendix B says the committee was not tasked to conduct a systematic review but adopted key features of one: six searches of Medline, Embase and the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (and PsycINFO for one) for January 1999 to 2 August 2016, quality assessment by more than one person (systematic reviews rated good, fair or poor by at least two members; primary studies guided by the Cochrane tool and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale), questions pre-specified before conclusions, standard wording for the strength of evidence (conclusive, substantial, moderate, limited, no or insufficient; Box B-3) and National Academies conflict-of-interest procedures. Existing systematic reviews were used first, then primary studies. In the chapters read the committee pools nothing itself.
can_establish: What an expert committee concluded in January 2017, from searches that closed on 2 August 2016, about the strength of published evidence on statistical associations between cannabis (mainly smoking) and lung function, COPD, respiratory symptoms and chronic bronchitis, asthma, lung cancer, and head and neck cancer; which studies it relied on, the limitations it named, and the research it asked for.
cannot_establish: Whether smoking cannabis causes any of these outcomes (every conclusion is worded as a statistical association and rests mostly on observational studies, many with self-reported use and without control for tobacco); the size of any effect (the grading hierarchy 'does not imply the magnitude of the observed effect' and the committee pools nothing); evidence published after 2 August 2016, including the 2018 meta-analysis and the 2022 Ontario cohort in this library; the effect of heavy daily smoking apart from tobacco; the effect of tobacco mixed into joints or of product strength; other forms of cannabis (vaping, edibles). For lung cancer it cannot settle the gap between its own wording and the Swedish cohort it describes (see reporting issues).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (literature review). Evidence base per Appendix B: Search 1 (Medline, Embase, Cochrane; January 1999 to June 2016) found 19,189 articles and was judged too broad; Searches 2 and 3 (2,092 and 7,198 articles) used narrower and then broader terms and excluded animal and 'spice' terms; Search 4 (PsycINFO, 1,396) covered mental health, Search 5 ('nabilone', 33) and Search 6 (389, extended to 2 August 2016) filled gaps; members also added articles from their own libraries. Articles were sorted into topic areas, then into 11 endpoint areas, and the committee chose the specific health endpoints to review.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Primary literature: peer-reviewed cross-sectional, case-control and cohort studies, randomised trials and non-systematic reviews; editorials, opinion pieces and grey literature were removed on reading abstracts. Weight by design: randomised trials first, then non-randomised controlled trials, prospective controlled studies and case-control studies, with case series and case studies only where nothing better existed (the list does not name cross-sectional studies, the commonest design in Chapter 7). Where a good or fair systematic review existed, primacy went to the most recent (since 2011) and only primary studies after its search date were added; where none existed all primary studies from 1 January 1999 to 2 August 2016 were reviewed. Chapter 7 found no fair- or good-quality systematic review since 2011 and 'elected to include' one from 2007 (literature through 2005).
sample.selection_effects: The committee narrowed a very large literature to chosen endpoints and says some literature may have been missed and that 'very good research may not be reflected' in the report. The search listing for Search 2 limits to English-language human studies from 1999 (other listings not read). The respiratory chapter rests on a 2007 systematic review plus 14 primary articles; the lung cancer evidence on one pooled analysis of six case-control studies (four unpublished) and one cohort; the head and neck evidence on one meta-analysis of nine case-control studies with no newer good-quality study. A committee member named Stephen Sidney (Kaiser Permanente Northern California) shares a name and initial with the 'Sidney S' listed among the authors of the CARDIA cohort paper the lung-function section relies on (Pletcher et al., 2012); the report does not comment (name match only).

exposure.measurement: Varies by cited study. The chapters say most studies relied on self-reported cannabis smoking without objective confirmation; a few used joint-years (1 joint a day for 1 year) or frequency in the past year; many did not control dose or duration, and lung-toxic content may vary 'from joint to joint'. Smoking technique, depth of inhalation and product strength are largely not recorded.
exposure.polysubstance: Tobacco and other inhaled drugs and occupational and environmental exposures are the main confounders, and the report says many studies did not control for them. The Swedish cohort did not account for tobacco or cannabis use during its 40 years of follow-up, and its authors did not know whether participants mixed tobacco and cannabis (as described in Chapter 5).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (observational studies of current and past use). Symptom studies compare people who stopped with people who continued.

comparison.controls: Varies: people who do not smoke, or who never used cannabis; low-use groups; groups smoking tobacco only in several lung and COPD studies; one study has no non-smoking group. The pooled lung-cancer analysis compares habitual with non-habitual cannabis smoking, the latter defined as under 1 joint-year including people who never used cannabis (Chapter 5, footnote 1).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not assessed by the committee beyond naming confounding. The report says cancer studies often lacked family history, occupational exposures and diet, and that cancer's long incubation needs long follow-up (Chapter 5, Summary, paragraph after Box 5-1).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Mostly not controlled; the committee lists 'tobacco and other inhaled drugs' among unadjusted confounders (Chapter 7, pulmonary function, Discussion, 1st paragraph).

outcomes.instruments: Spirometry (FEV1, FVC, FEV1/FVC), lung volumes, airway conductance and resistance, diffusing capacity, CT lung density; COPD by FEV1/FVC below 0.7 or hospital readmission; symptoms (cough, phlegm, wheeze, chronic bronchitis, dyspnea) by questionnaire; asthma by self-report; lung cancer and head and neck cancer incidence from case-control and cohort data.
outcomes.operationalization: The committee's conclusions concern a 'statistical association' with each endpoint; they do not give a size of effect and do not claim causation.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical synthesis by the committee). Nine graded conclusions (numbered 7-1 to 7-4 with sub-parts, and 5-1 and 5-2) fall in the parts read.

analysis.effect_sizes: The committee pools nothing. Figures it reports from cited studies: lung cancer, pooled analysis of six case-control studies, habitual against non-habitual cannabis smoking OR 0.96 (95% CI 0.66 to 1.38); among people who did not smoke tobacco OR 1.03 (0.51 to 2.08); adenocarcinoma only, more than 1 joint a day OR 1.73 (0.75 to 4.00) and more than 10 joint-years OR 1.74 (0.85 to 3.56). Swedish conscripts followed 40 years, more than 50 occasions at conscription against never, HR 2.12 (1.08 to 4.14), adjusted for tobacco, alcohol, respiratory conditions and socioeconomic status at conscription. Head and neck cancer, nine case-control studies pooled: OR 1.021 (0.912 to 1.143). Symptoms: 2007 review, long-term smoking cough OR 1.7 to 2.0, sputum 1.5 to 1.9, wheeze 2.0 to 3.0; Dunedin cohort, frequent use, morning cough OR 1.97, sputum 2.31, wheeze 1.55; Tashkin 2012 cohort (299 people, 9.8 years), current against never use, cough OR 1.7, sputum 2.1, bronchitis episodes 2.3, wheeze 3.4. COPD: tobacco only 24.3% against tobacco and cannabis 25.2% (p = 0.90); NHANES, more than 20 joint-years, FEV1/FVC below 70% OR 2.1 (1.1 to 3.9).
analysis.covariates: Varies by cited study; the committee often notes that tobacco and occupational and environmental exposures were not controlled.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registered protocol is described; Appendix B says the questions of interest were pre-specified before conclusions were formulated.
analysis.selective_reporting: The committee chose which primary studies to describe (14 for the respiratory chapter; three primary articles for the whole cancer chapter) and shows no per-study quality ratings. The lung cancer text reports a positive cohort estimate while its conclusion points the other way (see reporting issues).
analysis.power: Not applicable. The committee notes small numbers of people who smoked heavily in the cited studies (CARDIA; the pooled lung-cancer analysis).

interpretation_gap.results_show: What the chapters describe: cough, phlegm, wheeze and bronchitis episodes are more frequent in people who smoke cannabis than in people who do not, in cross-sectional studies and a few cohorts, mostly with self-reported use and incomplete control for tobacco, and fell after stopping in two cohorts, one with high loss to follow-up; lung-function results are inconsistent (short-term airway widening; higher lung volumes; no consistent loss of FEV1; a lower FEV1/FVC ratio at more than 20 joint-years in one national survey that is partly explained by the higher FVC); COPD and asthma studies are few, small or cross-sectional; for lung cancer a pooled analysis of case-control studies found no significant association, with an interval that includes a 38% rise and imprecise estimates at heavy use, while a Swedish cohort found a doubled hazard in those who reported using cannabis more than 50 times at conscription; for head and neck cancer a meta-analysis of case-control studies found no association in the pooled estimate, and its authors judged the evidence insufficient.
interpretation_gap.claimed: Graded conclusions (the committee's judgments): symptoms 'substantial' (7-3a) and stopping 'moderate' (7-3b); acute airway widening 'moderate' and higher FVC 'moderate' (7-1); COPD in people who smoke cannabis occasionally, controlled for tobacco 'limited' (7-2a) and COPD admissions 'insufficient' (7-2b); asthma 'no or insufficient' (7-4); lung cancer and head and neck cancer 'moderate evidence of no statistical association' (5-1, 5-2). Beyond these, the Chapter 5 highlight says the evidence suggests smoking cannabis 'does not increase the risk' of lung and head and neck cancer; the Chapter 7 highlight says 'Quitting cannabis smoking is likely to reduce chronic cough and phlegm production'; and the Chapter 7 Summary says respiratory risks 'appear to be relatively small' and 'far lower than those of tobacco smoking'. Gaps: (1) the cancer highlight is stronger than the graded wording, which is about statistical significance; the pooled lung-cancer interval (0.66 to 1.38) does not exclude a rise, the chapter reports a hazard ratio of 2.12 and says other reviewed studies 'indicate an increased risk', whereas Box B-3 asks for 'very few or no credible opposing findings' for 'moderate'; (2) for head and neck cancer the committee's grade is stronger than the review authors' own conclusion that evidence was insufficient; (3) the quitting highlight uses causal wording over an association graded on cohorts with loss to follow-up; (4) the tobacco comparison in the Summary is not a numbered conclusion, and the chapter holds pieces pointing both ways (per joint, a 339-person cross-sectional study estimated a lower FEV1/FVC equal to that of 2.5 to 5 cigarettes, an analysis the committee itself criticises, and 15 volunteers took in more carbon monoxide and tar per joint; per day, people who smoke cannabis usually smoke fewer cannabis cigarettes than people who smoke tobacco smoke cigarettes) without showing how they were weighed; (5) Conclusion 7-2(a) says 'occasional' smoking while the Discussion calls the link unclear for regular use and cites a position statement of minimal impairment in people who smoke cannabis occasionally.

timeline.event: Wu et al.: 15 volunteers, one joint gave about four times the carbon monoxide exposure and three to five times the tar deposition of one cigarette (as described in this report's Chapter 7).

The Institute of Medicine's earlier report concluded that cannabis smoking was an important risk factor for respiratory disease and that bronchitis may result from chronic use (as described in this report's Chapter 7).
Tetrault et al. systematic review (literature through 2005): the respiratory chapter's main systematic review.
CARDIA cohort, 20 years: occasional and low cumulative smoking not associated with lower lung function; used by this report.
Swedish military conscript cohort, 40 years: HR 2.12 for the highest cannabis group (as described in this report's Chapter 5; the paper itself is not yet read in this library).

Pooled analysis of six case-control studies of lung cancer (Zhang et al.), meta-analysis of head and neck cancer (de Carvalho et al.) and the American Thoracic Society position statement (Douglas et al.), all used by this report.
Critical review of this report by Cousijn and colleagues
Systematic review and meta-analysis to April 2018: symptom evidence 'low' strength, lung-function evidence 'insufficient' on its own scale
Ontario linked-data cohort: no excess respiratory emergency visits or admissions over 12 months

replication.where_it_stands: A consensus review is not replicated as such. Later work in this library: the 2018 meta-analysis rated the same symptom evidence 'low' on the AHRQ scale and lung function 'insufficient' (different scales from the committee's, not a contradiction of direction); the 2022 Ontario cohort found no excess respiratory emergency visits; the Swedish cohort and the pooled lung-cancer analysis have not been replicated in the sources read. The committee itself asks for replication because 'many associations are based on single studies'.

funding.funder: Sponsors listed in the Acknowledgments: Alaska Mental Health Trust Authority; Arizona Department of Health Services; California Department of Public Health; CDC Foundation; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention; The Colorado Health Foundation; Mat-Su Health Foundation; National Highway Traffic Safety Administration; National Institutes of Health (National Cancer Institute; National Institute on Drug Abuse); Oregon Health Authority; the Robert W. Woodruff Foundation; Truth Initiative; US Food and Drug Administration; Washington State Department of Health.
funding.declared_conflicts: Appendix B says conflicts of interest were declared under the National Academies conflict-of-interest policies; the individual declarations are not in the parts read.
funding.affiliations_note: A committee of 16 academics (Harvard, UCSF, Johns Hopkins, Columbia, Kaiser Permanente Northern California and others, as listed). No cannabis- or tobacco-industry sponsor is listed in the Acknowledgments. One committee member's name matches a co-author of a cohort the lung-function section relies on (see selection effects). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the report.

what_would_settle_it: Cohorts of people who smoke cannabis with objective and repeated measures of use, product content and tobacco mixing, followed for decades with spirometry, imaging and cancer-registry linkage, large enough in heavy use and compared with people who smoke tobacco only and people who use neither. The committee itself asks for better observational studies with self-reported and quantitative measures of dose and duration, longitudinal studies for asthma and allergy, and trials of other inhaled forms against smoking.

domains.note: A documented multi-database search and an explicit hierarchy, with systematic reviews first; but the report says it was not a systematic review, narrowed the literature to committee-chosen endpoints, may have missed literature, and shows only the studies it judged best (14 primary respiratory articles; three primary articles in the whole cancer chapter). The respiratory chapter rests on a 2007 review.

Methods named (Box B-2 questions rated by at least two members; Cochrane tool and Newcastle-Ottawa Scale), and the text names limitations of most studies and catches a labelling error in one; but no per-study ratings are shown, so 'good- to fair-quality' cannot be traced to a study.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: No sign that the committee relied on its own work; one committee member's name matches a co-author of one cited cohort (CARDIA).

Graded conclusions are separate from discussion, but the chapter highlights and the respiratory Summary go beyond them: a causal 'likely to reduce' over an association, a cancer highlight stronger than 'no statistical association', and a comparison with tobacco that is not a numbered conclusion.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against harm
domains.note: Both sides are described, including the Swedish cohort and the symptom studies, but the lung cancer grade sits uneasily with the contrary evidence described in the same chapter and with the committee's own definition of 'moderate'; the head and neck grade is stronger than the review authors' own conclusion.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard risk-of-bias instrument applies to a consensus review (METHODS section 5.3 lists none), so the editors' narrative-review checklist is used. This is a documented, multi-database, cautiously worded committee review whose respiratory conclusions follow the studies it describes. Its weaker points for this library are the cancer wording (a grade of 'no statistical association' over a pooled estimate that does not exclude a rise and a cohort that points up) and highlights that go beyond the numbered conclusions. It may be cited for the committee's graded wording as the committee's, for the list of studies under each conclusion with their sizes and limitations, and for its research gaps; claims should cite the primary studies and later reviews it summarises, not use its highlights as findings.

key_findings.finding: Method, search: six searches of Medline, Embase and the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (PsycINFO for Search 4) covering January 1999 to 2 August 2016; Searches 2 to 6 were combined into a master library of 10,759 unique articles (1,488 first categorised as systematic reviews), sorted into 11 endpoint areas; filtering to the chosen endpoints left 6,540 primary articles and 288 systematic reviews. The Search 2 listing limits to English-language human studies from 1999.
key_findings.locator: Appendix B › Literature Search, 1st to 6th paragraphs (from 'A professional research librarian' to 'After filtering the original search results'); Search Strategies (Search 2)

key_findings.finding: Method, appraisal: possible systematic reviews were screened with six questions, then rated good, fair or poor on five attributes adapted from the Cochrane group by at least two members independently (disagreements settled by deliberation or a third member); only good or fair reviews informed the report. Primary studies were reviewed guided by the Cochrane tool for randomised trials and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for cohort and case-control studies. The report says the committee was not tasked to conduct a systematic review and that literature may have been missed.
key_findings.locator: Appendix B › Literature Search, 7th to 9th paragraphs; Box B-2; Primary Literature: Identification and Quality Review, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Method, wording of conclusions: evidence was privileged in the order randomised trials, non-randomised controlled trials, prospective controlled studies, case-control studies, with case series only when nothing better. The weight of evidence was decided in private deliberations of committee subgroups. Box B-3 defines 'substantial' (several supportive findings from good-quality studies, very few or no credible opposing findings), 'moderate' (several from good- to fair-quality studies, very few or no credible opposing findings; limitations including chance, bias and confounding cannot be ruled out), 'limited' (fair-quality studies or mixed findings with most favouring one conclusion; significant uncertainty) and 'no or insufficient' (mixed findings, a single poor study, or not studied). The hierarchy 'does not imply the magnitude of the observed effect'.
key_findings.locator: Appendix B › Data Synthesis and Strength of Evidence Assessment, 1st paragraph; Box B-3

key_findings.finding: Respiratory symptoms (Conclusion 7-3): 'substantial evidence of a statistical association' (7-3a) between long-term cannabis smoking and worse respiratory symptoms and more frequent chronic bronchitis episodes, and 'moderate evidence' (7-3b) of an association between stopping and improvement. Under it: a 2007 systematic review of 14 symptom studies (nine cross-sectional, three case series, one case-control, one cohort; cough OR 1.7 to 2.0, sputum 1.5 to 1.9, wheeze 2.0 to 3.0); a Wellington cross-sectional study (cough 29% against 5%, wheeze 27% against 11%, chronic bronchitis symptoms 19% against 3%, people who smoked cannabis against people who did not); the Dunedin cohort of 1,037 followed to age 38 (frequent use, defined as 52 or more times in the past year: morning cough OR 1.97, sputum 2.31, wheeze 1.55; fewer symptoms after quitting); an internet survey of 5,987 adults recruited through drug-policy-reform organisations; a longitudinal cohort of 299 followed at least two visits over 9.8 years, with high or variable loss to follow-up (current against never use: cough OR 1.7, sputum 2.1, bronchitis episodes 2.3, wheeze 3.4; current against former use: cough 3.3, sputum 4.2, wheeze 2.1). The committee notes no clear additive effect of smoking both cannabis and tobacco on symptoms.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 7 › Respiratory Symptoms, Including Chronic Bronchitis › Systematic Reviews; Primary Studies (paragraphs on Aldington, Hancox 2015, Walden and Earleywine, Tashkin 2012); Discussion of Findings, 1st paragraph; Conclusion 7-3

key_findings.finding: Limits of the symptom evidence as the committee states them: most studies relied on self-reported cannabis smoking; many did not control for tobacco and occupational or environmental exposures, or for dose or duration; joint-years were rarely used and the THC content of a joint varies 'from joint to joint and from year to year'; Dunedin classed fewer than 52 uses a year as non-use and did not know whether cannabis was smoked; the internet survey recruited through organisations advocating drug-policy reform.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 7 › Respiratory Symptoms › Primary Studies (paragraphs after Figure 7-1 on Hancox 2015 limitations and on Walden and Earleywine); Discussion of Findings, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Lung function (Conclusion 7-1): 'moderate evidence' of an association between cannabis smoking and improved airway dynamics with acute use but not chronic use (7-1a) and with higher FVC (7-1b); the chapter highlight says it is unclear whether cannabis use is associated with worsened lung function. Under it: the 2007 review (34 publications; acute bronchodilation; regular smoking associated with lower specific airway conductance, about 16% on average, and a lower FEV1; inconsistent findings otherwise); CARDIA, 5,115 adults over 20 years, occasional and low cumulative smoking not associated with adverse effects on lung function, with a trend to lower FEV1 only at the heaviest exposure (20 or more joint-years) and with few people at heavy exposure; Dunedin (1,037, spirometry at 32): cumulative cannabis associated with higher FVC, total lung capacity and residual volume but not lower FEV1 or FEV1/FVC; NHANES 2007 to 2012 (10,327 adults, cross-sectional): lower FEV1/FVC and higher FEV1 and FVC in people who had smoked cannabis recently; a 12-person vaporizer feasibility study with no control group.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 7 › Pulmonary Function › Systematic Reviews; Primary Studies (paragraphs on Aldington, Papatheodorou, Pletcher, Hancox 2010, Van Dam and Earleywine); Discussion of Findings, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Conclusion 7-1; Chapter Highlights

key_findings.finding: COPD (Conclusion 7-2): 'limited evidence' of an association between occasional cannabis smoking and developing COPD when controlled for tobacco (7-2a); 'insufficient evidence' for hospital admissions for COPD (7-2b). Under it: a 339-person Wellington CT study with inconsistent results; Vancouver cross-sectional study of 878 adults (at least 50 cannabis cigarettes and no tobacco history: not at significantly greater risk of COPD or more respiratory symptoms; tobacco plus cannabis not clearly different from tobacco only); a 709-person readmission study (cannabis 0.22 against tobacco 0.26, unit not specified); a 500-person cross-sectional study with no non-smoking group (COPD 24.3% tobacco only against 25.2% tobacco plus cannabis, p = 0.90; more cough, phlegm and wheeze with both, no adjusted comparison); NHANES (more than 20 joint-years, FEV1/FVC below 70% OR 2.1, 95% CI 1.1 to 3.9, but higher FVC and no FEV1 association, and pre-bronchodilator spirometry). The Discussion says it is unclear whether regular use is associated with developing or worsening COPD and cites a position statement of minimal impairment in people who smoke cannabis occasionally once tobacco is controlled for.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 7 › Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease › Systematic Reviews; Primary Studies (paragraphs on Aldington, Tan 2009, Yadavilli, Macleod, Kempker); Discussion of Findings, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Conclusion 7-2

key_findings.finding: Asthma (Conclusion 7-4): 'no or insufficient evidence' to support or refute an association between cannabis smoking and asthma development or exacerbation, from a 506-boy cohort that found no link to self-reported asthma symptoms, a cohort of 110 adolescents with asthma that found no association with asthma concern, severity or symptoms, and one case-control letter of 100 emergency department patients that found no association with THC. The Discussion adds that wheeze appears common among people who use cannabis.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 7 › Asthma › Systematic Reviews; Primary Studies; Discussion of Findings, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Conclusion 7-4

key_findings.finding: Chapter 7 Summary and gaps: the committee writes that the risks of respiratory complications of cannabis smoking 'appear to be relatively small' and 'far lower than those of tobacco smoking', that people who smoke heavily may be at higher risk of chronic bronchitis and COPD but 'current studies do not provide sufficient evidence for a link', and names the limitations (cannabis and tobacco hard to separate; self-reported exposure; few cohorts of people who smoke regularly or daily; inadequate control of environmental factors; generalisability). Unknown, it says: whether long-term cannabis smoking above tobacco causes faster lung-function decline, chronic bronchitis or COPD; whether it raises the risk of allergic disease or asthma; whether other inhaled forms cause fewer respiratory symptoms.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 7 › Summary, 1st paragraph; Research Gaps, 1st paragraph and bullets

key_findings.finding: Background given for smoke exposure: in 15 volunteers one cannabis joint gave about four times the carbon monoxide exposure and three to five times the tar deposition of a single cigarette, with deeper inhalation, longer breath-holding and no filters; against this, cannabis cigarettes are less densely packed and people who use cannabis usually smoke fewer of them per day than people who smoke tobacco smoke cigarettes.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 7 › opening text (before Pulmonary Function), 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Lung cancer (Conclusion 5-1): 'moderate evidence of no statistical association between cannabis smoking and the incidence of lung cancer'. Under it: a pooled analysis of six case-control studies (four unpublished) with 2,159 cases and 2,985 controls found habitual against non-habitual cannabis smoking OR 0.96 (95% CI 0.66 to 1.38), and OR 1.03 (0.51 to 2.08) in people who did not smoke tobacco; risk rose with duration and intensity but not significantly; in adenocarcinoma alone, more than 1 joint a day OR 1.73 (0.75 to 4.00) and more than 10 joint-years OR 1.74 (0.85 to 3.56), 'suggestive' but not significant. An epidemiologic review (no meta-analysis) is said to include studies that 'indicate an increased risk'; its one cohort, 49,321 Swedish military conscripts followed 40 years (44,257 in the cannabis analysis), found HR 2.12 (95% CI 1.08 to 4.14) for more than 50 uses at conscription against never, adjusted for tobacco, alcohol, respiratory conditions and socioeconomic status at conscription. Habitual smoking was defined as at least 1 joint-year; non-habitual as under 1 joint-year, including people who never used cannabis.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 5 › Lung Cancer › Systematic Reviews; Primary Literature; Discussion of Findings, 1st paragraph; Conclusion 5-1; Footnotes 1 and 2

key_findings.finding: Limits of the lung cancer evidence as the committee states them: the pooled analysis could not account for differences in smoking technique or in the cannabis smoked, had too few people with heavy long-term smoking for precise estimates, and relied on self-report without biological validation; in the Swedish cohort detailed cannabis and tobacco use before and after baseline was lacking, tobacco and cannabis were not accounted for during the 40-year follow-up, its authors did not know whether participants mixed tobacco and cannabis, and self-reports were not anonymous.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 5 › Lung Cancer › Discussion of Findings, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Head and neck cancer (Conclusion 5-2): 'moderate evidence of no statistical association'. Under it: one meta-analysis of nine case-control studies (13,931 people; 5,732 cases, 8,199 controls) adjusted for tobacco, age, gender and race, OR 1.021 (0.912 to 1.143), whose authors concluded there was 'insufficient epidemiological evidence' to support a positive or negative association; no newer good-quality primary study; a null grouped result does not exclude associations with specific cancer types, and differences in methods prevented analysis of frequency, duration or method of use.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 5 › Head and Neck Cancers › Systematic Reviews; Primary Literature; Discussion of Findings, 1st paragraph; Conclusion 5-2

key_findings.finding: Chapter 5 gaps and summary: the committee judged the evidence on lung and head and neck cancer 'moderate' for 'no statistically significant association', lists small samples, low participation, unverifiable self-reported use and difficulty controlling confounders (family history, occupational exposures and diet often not accounted for) as common problems, says the long incubation of cancer needs long observation, and asks for studies that 'confirm existing evidence on lung and head and neck cancers' and for replication because exposures are changing and 'many associations are based on single studies'.
key_findings.locator: Chapter 5 › Research Gaps, bullets; Summary, 1st paragraph; paragraphs after Box 5-1

reporting_issues.issue: Chapter 5, head and neck Discussion: 'The systematic review also relied on cohort studies', although the same section describes the review (de Carvalho et al.) as nine case-control studies.
reporting_issues.consequence: The stated limitation (cohort studies may miss smaller or later-emerging risks) does not match the designs described; it is unclear which limitation was meant.

reporting_issues.issue: Conclusion 5-2 (head and neck) grades the evidence 'moderate evidence of no statistical association', while the review it rests on, quoted in the same section, concluded there was insufficient epidemiological evidence to support a positive or negative association.
reporting_issues.consequence: The committee's grade and the review authors' conclusion are not equivalent; cite each as its holder's.

reporting_issues.issue: Conclusion 5-1 (lung cancer) is graded 'moderate evidence of no statistical association', yet Box B-3 asks for very few or no credible opposing findings for 'moderate', and the chapter reports a cohort with HR 2.12 (1.08 to 4.14), says studies in the epidemiologic review but not in the pooled analysis 'indicate an increased risk', and gives adenocarcinoma estimates of about 1.7 that were not significant. The chapter does not explain how these were weighed.
reporting_issues.consequence: 'No statistical association' here means not statistically significant in a pooled estimate whose interval (0.66 to 1.38) does not exclude a rise; it is not a finding that smoking cannabis does not raise the risk.

reporting_issues.issue: The Chapter 5 highlight (the evidence 'suggests that smoking cannabis does not increase the risk' of lung and head and neck cancer) is stronger than Conclusions 5-1 and 5-2.
reporting_issues.consequence: Do not use the highlight as a finding; cite the numbered conclusion and the studies under it.

reporting_issues.issue: The Chapter 7 highlight 'Quitting cannabis smoking is likely to reduce chronic cough and phlegm production' uses causal wording, while Conclusion 7-3(b) grades only a statistical association between stopping and improvement, from cohorts with substantial loss to follow-up.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite 7-3(b) and the cohorts, not the highlight.

reporting_issues.issue: Conclusion 7-2(a) refers to 'occasional' cannabis smoking and 'limited evidence' of an increased risk of developing COPD when tobacco is controlled for; the Discussion calls the link unclear for regular use, and the position statement it cites found minimal impairment in people who smoke cannabis occasionally. The studies described do not show an association in people who smoke cannabis occasionally (the Vancouver study found no significantly greater risk; the 500-person study found no difference; the NHANES association was at more than 20 joint-years).
reporting_issues.consequence: The basis for the word 'occasional' in 7-2(a) is not apparent in the text read; use with care.

reporting_issues.issue: The Chapter 7 Summary states the respiratory risks of cannabis smoking are 'far lower than those of tobacco smoking'. This is not a numbered conclusion, and the sections read give no study that compares the two with the same measures at matched exposure; they give fewer joints per day, a position statement, and, pointing the other way, per-joint smoke exposure in 15 volunteers and an estimate (from an analysis the committee criticises) of a lower FEV1/FVC per joint equal to 2.5 to 5 cigarettes.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite as the committee's overall judgment, not as a measured comparison.

reporting_issues.issue: NHANES paragraph (Papatheodorou et al.): the group sizes (never 4,794; past 4,084; 5 to 30 days 555; 0 to 4 days 891) add to 10,324, not the 10,327 stated; and the effects given 'respectively' (FEV1/FVC -0.01 and -0.02; FEV1 49 and 89 mL; FVC 159 and 204 mL) are said to compare 'current smokers' with 'never smokers' without naming which two current groups the pairs belong to.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: the pairs cannot be assigned to groups from the text; check the primary paper before quoting.

reporting_issues.issue: Appendix B lists the order of evidence as randomised trials, non-randomised controlled trials, prospective controlled studies and case-control studies, but does not place cross-sectional studies, the commonest design in Chapter 7, and a chapter-7 conclusion of 'substantial' rests largely on cross-sectional data (nine of 14 studies in the 2007 review).
reporting_issues.consequence: How cross-sectional evidence was weighted for the grade is not stated.
